analysis.one_liner: Exempts private price-fixing and monopoly agreements from all federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have legalized price-fixing and monopolies among private parties, died in the Senate Judiciary Committee with zero cosponsors and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would declare that the nation's three main antitrust laws — the Sherman Act, the Clayton Act, and the FTC Act — do not apply to any voluntary agreement, contract, or cooperation between people or companies. In practice, that would mean companies could agree to fix prices, divide up markets, or merge into monopolies without the government being able to stop them. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and industry groups that want to coordinate on prices, divide territories, or consolidate without legal challenge. Dominant firms would gain the most, since antitrust law is the main check on their market power. Workers and consumers who might theoretically 'coordinate' with each other gain little, because the bill applies the same exemption to them but leaves them facing concentrated sellers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that the Sherman Act, the Clayton Act, and section 5 of the FTC Act 'shall not be construed to prohibit, ban, or otherwise extend to' any voluntary economic coordination, agreement, contract, or covenant between individuals or groups [S3].

The Congressional Research Service summary confirms the bill would bar these antitrust and unfair-competition laws from applying to voluntary economic coordination, cooperation, or agreement between any individual or group [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and workers. Price-fixing agreements raise the prices people pay for everyday goods, and unchallenged monopolies reduce quality and choice. Small businesses that compete with coordinated larger firms would also lose ground, since they would face rivals allowed to fix prices among themselves.

drawbacks.text: The core drawback is built into the design: the Sherman Act and Clayton Act exist to stop private agreements that raise prices and eliminate competition [S3]. Exempting 'any voluntary economic coordination' would remove the legal basis for challenging cartels, price-fixing rings, and monopolization, which standard economic analysis associates with higher consumer prices.

The bill is written without limits — it exempts coordination 'between any individual or group of individuals,' with no carve-out for mergers-to-monopoly, labor markets, or consumer protection, so even a supporter would have to acknowledge it sweeps far beyond any narrow libertarian goal of protecting voluntary association.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a principled argument — that people should be free to make voluntary agreements — but the cost would fall on the public in the form of legalized price-fixing and monopolies, while the main beneficiaries would be firms with market power. The one-sided drafting (no exceptions of any kind) makes the costs dominant.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no cosponsors and no action until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill in the Senate on March 5, 2018 [S1].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, its only committee assignment [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its lifetime [S4].
The record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers and workers are better off that the bill died, since it would have removed the laws that let the government challenge price-fixing and monopolies. No concentrated interest gained anything from the outcome.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing or markup — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, and the bill's sole sponsor was a Republican with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern can be measured [S4].

industries.industry: Large dominant firms and cartel-prone industries
industries.note: The bill would exempt all voluntary coordination from antitrust law, letting dominant firms fix prices, divide markets, and consolidate without legal challenge [S3]. Their gain would come directly out of consumer prices and choices.

Small firms compete against larger rivals and rely on antitrust enforcement as one of the few checks on coordinated market power [S3]. Exempting coordination would tilt the field further toward large, organized players.
